description: A chaotic and spontaneous group that rises to the challenge no matter the difficulty and still looks stylish while tackling it together.
summary:
Field profiles drawn live from open data. 
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

One block of farmland, rendered as an interactive 3D cut block: real terrain on top, the soil by depth on the cut faces, a long-term average month in the air above, and today's actual weather in the sky over the block (sun where it really is, clouds, rain, lightning when a storm is passing). Around the block, every number on the plate names its source, and where sources disagree, the plate shows the disagreement instead of hiding it.

Two live plates: Overberg and Swartland, Western Cape, are where the lead sites for the question the tool is built around: next winter, wheat on wheat again, or a lupin/canola break crop?
details:
Fallow helps a wheat grower or adviser in South Africa’s Western Cape think through one decision: next winter, do I plant wheat on wheat again, or put in a lupin or canola break crop? The page compares the two rotations side by side for the Overberg. Every fact on each card shows its source and a status of checked, unverified or assumed. Facts we could not source are marked “assumed, no source found” rather than filled in.

The main way Fallow handles uncertainty is the rain cross-check. Annual rainfall is shown from four sources on one scale: NASA GPM IMERG, Open-Meteo, ERA5 and Meteomatics. Open-Meteo and ERA5 come from the same ECMWF reanalysis, so the page says they are not independent. When the sources spread by more than 15% of the IMERG value, the page shows every value, gives Low confidence and offers no single verdict. The Swartland is included as an example of this. Its four sources differ by 182 mm a year, which is 48%. Users can also set their own priorities and see a weighted score, with every sub-score visible. The page also shows the ARC wheat trial as a trade-off and states its limits, since the break crop gave lower wheat yield in 7 of 9 trial cells but this does not count break-crop income, disease relief or nitrogen credit.

We used NASA GPM IMERG for rainfall, NASA POWER for humidity and temperature, and NASADEM/SRTM for terrain. Cross-checks came from SoilGrids, Copernicus DEM and Fields of the World field outlines. The page is static HTML with inlined data files, so it opens offline with no login and no third-party requests. A 3D field viewer is included for the field view. AI agents did much of the building and our team reviewed and checked the numbers against the data files. [AI use disclosure: confirm wording.]

The intended impact is a clearer view of options, not a recommendation. The page does not predict yield and does not tell anyone what to plant. We have not tested it with farmers or against field trials, and the page says so. Only one of the eight comparison scores has a sourced value, so the score is labelled illustrative and not validated.
